rationale: A wins because it turns the supplied weak spots into real editorial pressure, especially “Databricks graded its own model, and that is the part enterprises should check.” B is usable, but it smuggles in timing with “signaling an IPO it won't put a date on” and overstates the buyer premise with “cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API.” A has sharper beat separation and better kill conditions; B has good bones but needs a fact-cleaning pass before it goes near a reporter list.
gaps_in_A: “Databricks bets regulated enterprises would rather host a model than call one” overreaches slightly: the update says open license and fine-tuning on own data, not necessarily self-hosting or on-prem deployment.
“open weights mean third parties can begin reproducing them immediately” assumes open weights from open-sourcing/open license; likely, but the update does not state that exact release form.
“What a $3B private company gives away for free” treats open license as free distribution. That may be true, but the license terms are explicitly one of the facts still needing proof.
gaps_in_B: “The revenue figure and the IPO signal were disclosed alongside today's model release” invents timing. The update says Databricks has signaled an eventual IPO, not that the signal happened in this announcement.
“For banks and hospitals” names sectors the update did not supply. They are plausible regulated buyers, but this should be framed as examples to verify, not as established protagonists.

“cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API” and “inside its own perimeter” turn Databricks' positioning into buyer fact. That is exactly the claim a reporter would test, not something the angle gets to assume.
B misses the cleanest contrarian angle hiding in the update: the benchmarks are the company's own. It mentions this as proof hygiene but fails to make it a standalone accountability story.
